intro: In 1920 the federal government was small enough that most Americans met it only at the post office. By 1973 it ran old-age pensions and hospital insurance, guaranteed home loans and bank deposits, built a forty-thousand-mile highway system, stationed soldiers on four continents, and had put men on the Moon. Between those two dates the country lived through the biggest economic collapse in its history, the largest war ever fought, and a thirty-year standoff with the Soviet Union in which both sides kept enough weapons to end human life. Nearly every argument about government that Americans have today began in those fifty years.

This unit follows that story through people and places you can picture: a line outside a locked bank in a central Illinois town in March 1933; a squash court under the University of Chicago's football stands where the atomic age began in December 1942; a Japanese American family locking their farmhouse for a camp in the desert; a president reading photographs of missiles in Cuba over breakfast; and Michigan Avenue in August 1968, filled with tear gas and television cameras. Where the evidence allows, you will see the same event from more than one side: the worker and the owner, the general and the draftee, the senator and the witness he accused.

By the end you should be able to explain how the Depression and the war remade the federal government, how the Cold War shaped daily life from the suburbs to the schoolroom, and why Americans left this era more powerful, more prosperous and more divided than they had entered it. Most of all you should be able to argue, with dates, numbers and sources, about the question that runs through all three chapters: how much power should a government take in a crisis, and what should it give back when the crisis ends?
bigQuestion: From the Depression through Vietnam, Americans gave their government enormous new powers to fight crises at home and abroad. Did that power protect freedom, threaten it, or both?

test.q: Why did a bank run in March 1933 threaten even a sound bank?
choices: A bank lends out most of its deposits, so it cannot pay every depositor at once if they all demand cash
Banks were forbidden to hold cash
The government had already taken the deposits
Depositors could only withdraw gold
test.why: Banks keep only a small share of deposits as cash; a panic that brings everyone to the window at once empties the vault of even a healthy bank.

test.q: Which best describes the economy of the late 1920s that the crash of October 1929 exposed?
choices: Balanced and debt-free
Dominated by farm exports
Shrinking for most of the decade
Dependent on consumer credit and stock speculation, with farmers and many workers already struggling
test.why: Installment debt, margin buying and weak farm income meant the crash hit an economy with little cushion.

test.q: What was the main purpose of the 1924 immigration law?

To sharply cut immigration from southern and eastern Europe and bar it from Asia through national quotas
To recruit workers for Chicago factories
To end all immigration from Mexico
test.why: The quotas favored northern and western Europe and reflected the nativism that also fed the Klan's revival.

test.q: How did the Second New Deal of 1935 differ from the Hundred Days of 1933?
choices: It created lasting institutions such as Social Security and the right to unionize rather than emergency relief alone
It repealed most of the first New Deal
It focused only on banking
It was passed by Hoover
test.why: The 1933 laws answered the emergency; the 1935 laws built permanent structures that still exist.

test.q: What happened when Roosevelt proposed adding justices to the Supreme Court in 1937?

The Court resigned in protest
Roosevelt withdrew the plan before Congress saw it
Congress rejected the plan, but the Court soon began upholding New Deal laws anyway

The public expected war with Japan

Their own request for protection

With a Chinese surrender

The United Nations took control of the missiles

Medicare was repealed

title: U.S. History: World Wars and the Cold War

chapters.title: Boom, Bust and the New Deal
chapters.bigQuestion: When an economy collapses, what should a government do, and who gets to decide?

story.title: The Morning the Bank Did Not Open
story.kicker: In the first days of March 1933, people in small towns across Illinois lined up outside their banks before dawn, and then the doors stayed locked.
paragraphs: Picture a farm town in central Illinois on a cold Friday morning, March 3, 1933. The bank on the courthouse square opened at nine. By eight there was already a line. A hardware store owner stood with his account book. A widow held a passbook that showed the savings of thirty years. A farmer who had sold his corn for less than it cost to grow it wanted whatever was left. Nobody was shouting. They just wanted their money in their hands before it vanished.

A *bank run* works like this. A bank does not keep all its deposits in the vault. It lends most of the money out, to farmers for seed and to shopkeepers for stock, and keeps only a small share as cash. That is fine as long as people trust the bank. But if enough customers all demand their cash on the same day, the bank cannot pay them, even if its loans are sound. Fear alone can kill a healthy bank. Between 1930 and 1933 roughly nine thousand American banks failed, and every failure made people in the next town more afraid.

By early March 1933 the fear had reached the whole country. Governors in state after state ordered every bank closed to stop the panic. On Saturday, March 4, Franklin Roosevelt took the oath as president and told the crowd that the only thing the nation had to fear was fear itself. Two days later he declared a national bank holiday. Every bank in the United States, including the one on that courthouse square, was shut by order of the government.

Then something unusual happened. Congress passed an emergency banking law in a single day. Government examiners checked the books of each bank. On Sunday night, March 12, Roosevelt spoke on the radio to tens of millions of listeners, calmly explaining what a bank does and promising that the banks reopening on Monday were sound. On Monday morning, in that Illinois town and in thousands like it, the lines formed again. This time most people were bringing their money back.

That single week is the whole argument of this chapter in miniature. A crisis born of fear and bad rules. A government deciding to act in ways it never had before. Millions of people changing their minds because a leader explained things plainly. And a question that has never gone away: how much should the government do when the economy fails, and who pays for it?
story.think: The banks that reopened on March 13 had the same loans and the same cash as the week before. What actually changed, and why did it work?

lessons.title: Cars, Radio and Credit
lessons.mainIdea: Mass production, installment buying and radio changed daily life in the 1920s and tied the economy to consumer spending.
reading: In 1908 a new car cost more than most families earned in a year. By the mid-1920s a Ford Model T sold for under three hundred dollars, and a factory worker could buy one. Henry Ford did it with the moving *assembly line*: instead of a team building one car, the car moved past workers who each did one small job over and over. A Model T that once took more than twelve hours to build could be finished in about ninety minutes. The car remade the country. It needed paved roads, gas stations, motels and suburbs, and it let a farm family drive to a city they had never seen.

Most people still could not pay cash for a car, a washing machine or a radio. So businesses sold on *installment credit*: a small payment down, then monthly payments with interest. Buy now, pay later. By the end of the decade a large share of cars and household appliances were bought this way. Credit made the boom bigger, because families could spend money they had not earned yet. It also made the boom fragile. If wages fell or jobs vanished, the payments would still come due.

Radio arrived almost overnight. Station KDKA in Pittsburgh began regular broadcasts in 1920. Within a few years, families across the country gathered around a wooden set in the parlor to hear the same music, the same ballgames and the same advertisements at the same moment. For the first time a farm family in Illinois and an apartment in New York could share one national experience. Advertising on radio taught Americans to want the same products, which fed the consumer economy even more.

Not everyone shared the good years. Farmers had borrowed to expand during World War I, when Europe needed American grain. When European farms recovered, prices for corn and wheat collapsed, and farmers spent the whole decade in debt. Coal miners, textile workers and most Black Americans in the rural South saw little of the boom. The 1920s were roaring mostly in the cities and mostly for people with wages to spend.

words.d: a way of making things where the product moves past workers who each repeat one small task
buying something with a small payment down and the rest paid monthly with interest
an economy that depends on ordinary people buying goods for their own use

look.title: The Payment Book
look.text: A machinist in Rockford earns about thirty dollars a week in 1928. He owes twelve dollars a month on a used Ford, eight on a radio and six on a washing machine. His wife keeps the payment books in a kitchen drawer. In the fall of 1929 the plant cuts him to three days a week.
look.prompt: Trace what happens to his household, to the stores he owes, and to the bank that lent those stores money. How does one family's trouble spread?

check.q: Why did Ford's assembly line make cars cheaper?

Each worker repeated one small task, so cars were built much faster
Ford used cheaper metal than other companies
The government paid part of the cost
check.why: Moving the car past workers who each did one job cut building time from over twelve hours to about ninety minutes.

check.q: How did installment credit make the boom fragile?
choices: Families were spending money they had not yet earned, so lost wages meant missed payments
Stores refused to sell to workers
Interest rates were set by radio stations
It kept people from buying cars
check.why: Buy now, pay later works only while wages keep coming. When jobs vanished, the payments still came due.

choices: Radio station owners
City factory workers with steady wages
Automobile dealers
Farmers stuck in debt after crop prices collapsed
check.why: Farmers had borrowed during the war and spent the 1920s in debt as corn and wheat prices fell.

lessons.title: Jazz, Harlem and the Dry Decade
lessons.mainIdea: The 1920s produced a burst of Black art and music and a failed national experiment in banning alcohol.
reading: In 1922 a young cornet player named Louis Armstrong took a train from New Orleans to Chicago to join King Oliver's band on the South Side. Chicago's Black population had more than doubled during the Great Migration, and the clubs along State Street were packed. The music they played was *jazz*: fast, built on improvisation, rooted in blues and ragtime. Records and radio carried it to white audiences across the country. By the end of the decade jazz was the sound of the age, and the age took its name from it.

In New York, the neighborhood of Harlem became the center of a movement in writing, painting and thought that came to be called the *Harlem Renaissance*. Langston Hughes wrote poems in the rhythm of blues. Zora Neale Hurston collected the folk stories of the Black South. Writers and artists argued about what it meant to be Black and American at the same time, and they insisted that their own lives and voices were worthy subjects of art. Their work reached readers far beyond Harlem and shaped American literature for the rest of the century.

At the same time the country tried to stop drinking. The Eighteenth Amendment, in force from January 1920, banned making, selling or transporting alcohol. Supporters, many of them churchgoers and reformers, expected less crime, healthier families and safer workplaces. *Prohibition* did cut drinking for a while. But millions of people kept buying liquor from illegal bars called speakeasies, and supplying them became a huge criminal business. In Chicago, gangs led by men like Al Capone fought over the trade, and the city's violence made national headlines.

By 1933 most Americans had decided the experiment had failed. Enforcing the law was expensive, courts were clogged, and the money flowed to criminals instead of taxpayers. The Twenty-first Amendment repealed Prohibition that December. It remains the only amendment ever passed to cancel another one. Prohibition is worth remembering as a test of a hard question: when a law tries to change how millions of people live, what makes it work or fail?

words.d: American music built on improvisation, born in New Orleans from blues and ragtime
a movement of Black writers, artists and thinkers centered in Harlem, New York, in the 1920s
the period from 1920 to 1933 when the Constitution banned making and selling alcohol
an illegal bar during Prohibition

look.prompt: The amendment bans making, selling and transporting alcohol, but not drinking it. Why might the writers have left that out, and how would that gap shape enforcement?

check.q: Why did Louis Armstrong move to Chicago in 1922?

To escape Prohibition, which did not apply in Illinois
To join a band on the South Side, where the Great Migration had built a large Black community
To work in a car factory

choices: That art should avoid politics
That Black lives and voices were worthy subjects of serious art
That jazz should not be recorded
That Harlem should become a separate city

check.q: What makes the Twenty-first Amendment unusual?
choices: It was ratified in a single day
It was the first amendment about alcohol
It was written by Al Capone's lawyers
It is the only amendment that cancels another amendment

lessons.title: Nativism and the Klan's Return
lessons.mainIdea: Fear of immigrants, radicals and Black Americans drove strict immigration quotas and a huge revival of the Ku Klux Klan in the 1920s.
reading: The same decade that produced jazz also produced a wave of fear. Between 1890 and 1914 millions of immigrants had arrived from Italy, Poland, Russia and other parts of southern and eastern Europe. Many older Americans saw them as too Catholic, too Jewish, too poor or too radical. This attitude is called *nativism*: the belief that people born in the country deserve more than newcomers. After a Communist revolution in Russia in 1917 and a string of bombings in 1919, the fear turned to panic. In the Red Scare of 1919 and 1920, the government arrested thousands of suspected radicals and deported hundreds without trial.

Congress answered with the Immigration Act of 1924. It set a *quota* for each country, tied to how many people from that country had lived in the United States decades earlier. The effect was deliberate: large quotas for Britain and Germany, tiny ones for Italy and Poland, and none at all for Japan and most of Asia. Immigration from southern and eastern Europe fell sharply. The law stayed in force for forty years, and it later shut the door on many people fleeing Nazi Germany.

The Ku Klux Klan of the 1920s was different from the terror group of Reconstruction. Refounded in Georgia in 1915, it sold itself as a patriotic club for white Protestants and recruited with paid organizers and modern advertising. Its enemies were Black Americans, Catholics, Jews and immigrants. At its peak in the mid-1920s it claimed millions of members and had real political power, especially in Indiana, Oregon and Colorado, not just the South. Klan members held parades in daylight, elected mayors and governors, and marched down Pennsylvania Avenue in Washington in 1925.

The Klan collapsed almost as fast as it rose. In 1925 Indiana's Klan leader was convicted of the rape and death of a young woman, and members quit by the hundreds of thousands. The 1927 trial and execution of Sacco and Vanzetti, two Italian immigrant anarchists convicted of murder on thin evidence, showed the same fear at work in the courts. Historians read the 1920s as two Americas pulling against each other: one urban, diverse and modern, the other rural, Protestant and frightened of change.

words.d: the belief that people born in a country should be favored over immigrants
a fixed limit on how many people or things are allowed; here, immigrants per country per year
the panic over Communists and radicals in 1919 and 1920 that led to mass arrests and deportations

look.prompt: Four of the six strongest states are in the North or Midwest. What does that tell you about who the 1920s Klan was recruiting and what it was afraid of?

By a quota tied to how many people from that country had lived in the U.S. decades earlier
By lottery each year
Only people with jobs waiting could come
check.why: The quotas were designed to favor Britain and Germany and shrink immigration from Italy, Poland and Asia.

check.q: How was the 1920s Klan different from the Klan of Reconstruction?
choices: It recruited openly with paid organizers and was strong in northern states like Indiana
It only operated at night in the South
It welcomed Catholics and Jews as members
It had no interest in politics

check.q: Why do historians see the Sacco and Vanzetti case as part of the same story as the Klan?
choices: Both men were Klan members

lessons.title: October 1929
lessons.mainIdea: The stock market crash of 1929 did not cause the Depression by itself, but it exposed a weak economy built on debt and speculation.
reading: Through the late 1920s stock prices rose so fast that people who had never owned a share started buying. Many bought *on margin*: putting down as little as ten percent and borrowing the rest from a broker. If a stock went up, the buyer kept all the gain. If it went down, the broker demanded the loan back at once. By 1929 the market was a tower of borrowed money. Prices had little to do with what the companies actually earned. That is *speculation*: buying not because a thing is worth the price but because you expect someone else to pay more.

On Thursday, October 24, 1929, prices broke. Panicked selling on the New York Stock Exchange overwhelmed the tickers. A group of big bankers pooled money to buy stocks and calm the floor, and it worked for a day. On Tuesday, October 29, the selling came back and nothing could stop it. Sixteen million shares changed hands. Brokers called in margin loans; investors who could not pay were wiped out, and their forced selling drove prices lower still. By mid-November the market had lost roughly a third of its value.

Only a small minority of Americans owned any stock, so why did the crash matter to a farmer in Illinois? Because the economy underneath was already weak. Farm prices had been falling for a decade. Wages had not kept up with what factories produced, so warehouses were filling with unsold cars and radios. Wealth was concentrated at the top, and the middle had been spending on credit. When the crash destroyed confidence, families stopped buying, factories cut shifts, and the credit chain began to snap link by link.

Economists still argue about which cause mattered most. Was it the debt, the unequal incomes, the mistakes of the Federal Reserve, or the collapse of trade after new tariffs in 1930? What they agree on is that the crash turned a slowdown into a *depression*, a long period in which production, jobs and prices all fall together. It would last, in one form or another, for more than ten years.

words.d: buying stock with mostly borrowed money, putting down only a small share of the price
buying something only because you expect to sell it to someone else for more
a long, deep economic collapse in which production, jobs and prices all fall

look.title: Ten Percent Down
look.text: In 1929 a schoolteacher buys one hundred dollars of stock with ten dollars of her own money and ninety borrowed from a broker. In a week the stock rises to one hundred twenty. She has doubled her ten dollars. Then the stock falls to eighty. The broker demands his ninety dollars today.
look.prompt: Work out what she has left in each case. Why does margin make gains and losses so much larger, and what happens when thousands of brokers make that same call on the same morning?

check.q: What does it mean to buy stock on margin?
choices: To buy only stock in very safe companies
To buy stock through a bank instead of a broker
To pay a small share yourself and borrow the rest from a broker
To buy stock in a company you work for
check.why: Margin buyers might put down only ten percent, which magnified both gains and losses.

check.q: Why did the crash hurt people who owned no stock?
choices: Because the government took their savings to pay brokers
Because the underlying economy was weak and the crash destroyed confidence and credit
Because all banks were owned by stockbrokers
Because stock certificates were used as money
check.why: Falling confidence led families to stop buying and factories to cut jobs, which spread the damage far beyond investors.

check.q: What do economists agree on about the crash?
choices: That it was caused entirely by the Federal Reserve
That it did not affect farmers
That it was over by 1930
That it turned a slowdown into a long depression
check.why: Historians debate the causes but agree the crash marked the start of a collapse that lasted more than a decade.

lessons.title: Hard Times and Hoover
lessons.mainIdea: By 1933 a quarter of workers had no job, and President Hoover's limited responses left many Americans feeling abandoned.
reading: By 1932 the numbers were beyond anything the country had seen. About one worker in four had no job at all, and many more worked only a few days a week. In Chicago the city could not pay its teachers for months. Families who could not pay rent were evicted, and on the edges of cities people built shacks from scrap wood and tin. They called these camps *Hoovervilles*, after the president. Men rode freight trains looking for work. Breadlines stretched around blocks. In the countryside, farmers watched banks foreclose on land their families had worked for generations.

Herbert Hoover was not a do-nothing president, and he was not a cruel man. He had organized food relief that fed millions in Europe after World War I. But he believed deeply that direct government payments to individuals would weaken people's character and that recovery had to come from business. He urged companies to keep wages up and asked charities and local governments to care for the needy. By 1931 charities and cities were out of money. In 1932 Hoover signed a law creating the Reconstruction Finance Corporation to lend money to banks and railroads, hoping it would trickle down to workers.

The summer of 1932 broke what was left of his reputation. Thousands of World War I veterans, many with their families, camped in Washington to ask Congress to pay a bonus they had been promised for 1945 early. They called themselves the *Bonus Army*. The Senate said no. In July, Hoover ordered the Army to clear them out. Soldiers with tanks and tear gas burned the camp. Newsreels showed veterans being driven from the capital by the army they had served in. Hoover's defenders said the order was to clear only downtown; the public saw a president attacking the poor.

In November 1932 Franklin D. Roosevelt, the governor of New York, beat Hoover by a landslide, carrying forty-two of forty-eight states. Roosevelt had promised a New Deal for the American people but had been vague about what it meant. Four months passed between the election and the March inauguration. During those months the banks began to fail in earnest, and the country waited.

veterans of World War I who camped in Washington in 1932 to demand early payment of a promised bonus
when a lender takes property because the borrower cannot make the loan payments

look.title: Out of Work
look.cite: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics historical series, rounded
look.prompt: Unemployment fell after 1933 but rose again in 1938 and was still fifteen percent in 1940. What does that pattern suggest about how much the New Deal fixed and what it did not?

check.q: Why did Hoover resist direct government payments to the unemployed?
choices: He did not know how bad conditions were
He believed they would weaken people's character and that recovery should come from business
The Supreme Court had forbidden them
He wanted to save money for the Bonus Army
check.why: Hoover trusted charities, local governments and business loans rather than direct federal relief to individuals.

check.q: What was the Reconstruction Finance Corporation meant to do?
choices: Lend money to banks and railroads so recovery would trickle down
Pay the veterans' bonus
Build camps for the homeless
Buy farmland from struggling farmers
check.why: The RFC of 1932 lent to large institutions in hope that jobs would follow.

check.q: Why did the Bonus Army incident damage Hoover so badly?
choices: The veterans won their bonus and thanked Congress instead
Hoover personally led the troops
The public saw the army driving out poor veterans who had served the country
It caused the stock market crash
check.why: Newsreels of soldiers burning the veterans' camp made Hoover look heartless, whatever his actual orders were.

lessons.title: The Dust Bowl
lessons.mainIdea: Drought, plowed-up grassland and high winds turned the southern Plains into a dust bowl and drove hundreds of thousands off the land.
reading: On Sunday, April 14, 1935, the sky over the Oklahoma and Texas panhandles turned black in the middle of the afternoon. A wall of dust thousands of feet high rolled across the plains, and inside it people could not see their own hands. Cars stalled, chickens went to roost at noon, and families stuffed wet rags under doors. People called it Black Sunday. A reporter's phrase for the region stuck: the *Dust Bowl*.

The dust was not just bad luck. For fifty years farmers had plowed up the deep-rooted grass that held the soil of the southern Plains in place, planting wheat when prices were high during World War I and the 1920s. When a severe *drought* began in 1931 and lasted most of the decade, the bare topsoil dried to powder. The constant plains wind did the rest. In the worst storms, dust from Kansas fell on ships in the Atlantic Ocean. Children and old people died of dust pneumonia. Fields that had grown wheat grew nothing.

Hundreds of thousands of people left. Many headed west on Route 66 toward California, and whatever state they came from they were called Okies, rarely as a compliment. In California they found low wages in the fields, camps by the roadside and signs telling them to keep moving. Dorothea Lange's photographs for a federal agency, especially a 1936 picture of a worn mother with her children, showed the rest of the country what the migrants' lives looked like. Historians use those photographs as evidence, and also ask how the photographer's choices shaped what viewers felt.

The federal government responded with science. The Soil Conservation Service, created in 1935, taught farmers to plow along the contour of the land, leave stubble in the fields and plant rows of trees as windbreaks. The government also bought up some of the worst land and returned it to grass. When the rains came back at the end of the decade, the plains recovered, though the region's water and soil remain fragile. The Dust Bowl is a case study in how human choices and nature together can make a disaster.

lessons.title: The Hundred Days
lessons.mainIdea: In his first hundred days Roosevelt and Congress passed a flood of laws that put the federal government directly into banking, farming, industry and relief.
reading: Franklin Roosevelt took office on March 4, 1933, with the banks collapsing, and he moved faster than any president before him. He kept Congress in session for what became known as the *Hundred Days*. Fifteen major laws passed. The Emergency Banking Act let sound banks reopen under government inspection. The Glass-Steagall Act separated ordinary banking from stock speculation and created the *FDIC*, which insures deposits so that a bank failure no longer wipes out savings. Bank runs of the old kind essentially stopped. That insurance still protects your savings account today.

Roosevelt did not follow one clear theory. He called it bold, persistent experimentation: try something, and if it fails, admit it and try something else. Some programs paid people to work. The Civilian Conservation Corps put young men in camps planting trees and building trails in state and national parks, including in Illinois. The Public Works Administration built dams, schools and bridges. Others paid people not to produce. The Agricultural Adjustment Act paid farmers to leave fields empty so crop prices would rise, which meant plowing under crops while people went hungry.

The National Recovery Administration tried to end cutthroat competition by having each industry write codes setting prices, wages and hours. Businesses that signed displayed a blue eagle in their windows. The Tennessee Valley Authority, a government-owned company, built dams that brought electricity and flood control to one of the poorest regions of the country. Never before had the federal government run a business, hired the unemployed by the million or told farmers what to plant.

Roosevelt explained all of it on the radio. His *fireside chats*, delivered in a calm, plain voice as if he were sitting in the listener's living room, made millions feel that someone in Washington understood their lives. The chats are a lesson in communication. He explained what a bank does, why gold was leaving the country, what the new laws would try. Historians credit the chats with rebuilding trust as much as any law did.

the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, which guarantees bank deposits so savers are not wiped out by a bank failure

lessons.title: Work, Wages and Security
lessons.mainIdea: The Second New Deal of 1935 created lasting institutions: public jobs through the WPA, the right to unionize, and Social Security.
reading: In 1935 Roosevelt turned from emergency measures to programs meant to last. The Works Progress Administration, the *WPA*, became the largest employer in the country. Over eight years it hired millions of people, at wages set below private jobs so it would not compete with them, to build roads, airports, schools and parks. It also paid writers to record oral histories, artists to paint murals in post offices, and actors to stage plays. Many Chicago schools, bridges and park buildings from the 1930s are WPA work, and the stone stamp is still on them.

The Wagner Act of 1935 gave workers a legal right to form unions and bargain with employers, and it created a board to police unfair labor practices. Union membership tripled by the end of the decade. Then came the law Roosevelt considered his most important. The *Social Security* Act created old-age pensions paid for by a tax on workers and employers, insurance for the unemployed, and aid for the disabled and for poor children. For the first time the federal government promised that growing old or losing a job would not mean destitution.

The law had deep flaws, and they were not accidents. To win the votes of southern Democrats, Congress left farm workers and domestic servants out of the pension system. Those two categories held most Black workers in the South, so the promise did not reach them for decades. Women who worked in the home were covered only through husbands. Historians point to this as an example of how a reform can advance and exclude at the same time.

The New Deal also changed politics. Black voters, who had voted Republican since Lincoln, moved into the Democratic Party because relief programs, imperfect as they were, reached them. Union members, immigrants in the cities and farmers in the West joined them. This *New Deal coalition* elected Democrats for most of the next thirty years. Roosevelt himself won four elections, the only president to do so, and after his death the Constitution was amended to limit presidents to two terms.

the 1935 system of pensions, unemployment insurance and aid paid for by payroll taxes

lessons.title: Critics Left and Right
lessons.mainIdea: The New Deal was attacked from the right as socialism and from the left as too timid, and the loudest critics pushed Roosevelt further.
reading: Not everyone cheered. Business leaders and conservative Democrats formed the American Liberty League in 1934 to argue that the New Deal was destroying free enterprise, piling up debt and giving Washington powers the Constitution never granted. Many newspapers, including the Chicago Tribune, attacked Roosevelt daily. These critics argued that the government could not spend its way out of a depression and that regulations were keeping business from hiring. That argument has never stopped; you will hear versions of it in every election today.

The attack from the other side was louder and, to Roosevelt, more dangerous. Senator Huey Long of Louisiana, a brilliant and ruthless politician, said the New Deal had done nothing for the poor. His Share Our Wealth plan promised to take fortunes over a few million dollars and give every family a house, a car and a yearly income. By 1935 his clubs claimed millions of members, and he was planning to run for president. He was assassinated in September of that year.

Father Charles Coughlin, a Catholic priest in Michigan, drew tens of millions of radio listeners with attacks on bankers that turned, over time, into open hatred of Jews. Dr. Francis Townsend, a retired physician in California, proposed a pension of two hundred dollars a month for everyone over sixty, to be spent within thirty days. Millions of older Americans signed his petitions. Each movement showed how much pain the New Deal had not touched, and each pressed Roosevelt to do more, which helps explain Social Security and the higher taxes on the rich in 1935.

Reading these critics fairly matters. The right was correct that the New Deal expanded federal power far beyond anything in the past and that the debt grew. The left was correct that unemployment stayed high and that many of the poorest got little. Roosevelt's answer was that a democracy in crisis had to act, and that acting imperfectly beat not acting at all. Historians still weigh those claims, and so should you.

lessons.title: Labor Rises
lessons.mainIdea: Protected by the Wagner Act, industrial unions organized the auto and steel industries through sit-down strikes, and Chicago saw the cost.
reading: The Wagner Act gave workers a right on paper. Making it real took a fight. The old American Federation of Labor organized skilled workers by craft and had little interest in the millions of unskilled workers on assembly lines. In 1935 John L. Lewis of the United Mine Workers broke away to form what became the *CIO*, the Congress of Industrial Organizations, which organized every worker in an industry, skilled or not, Black or white, into one union.

The breakthrough came in Flint, Michigan. On December 30, 1936, workers at a General Motors plant stopped the line and refused to leave the building. A *sit-down strike* meant the company could not bring in replacement workers without physically removing the strikers, and removing them risked wrecking the machines. The men slept on car seats while their wives and supporters passed food through the windows. Police tried tear gas and were driven back. After forty-four days General Motors, the largest corporation in the world, recognized the union in February 1937. Auto workers' wages and conditions changed for a generation.

Steel was harder. Chicago's Republic Steel refused to sign. On Memorial Day, May 30, 1937, strikers and their families held a picnic and march near the plant on the far South Side. Chicago police opened fire on the crowd. Ten marchers were killed, most shot in the back or side, and dozens more were wounded. A newsreel camera recorded it. A Senate committee later concluded the police had used far more force than the situation called for. The Memorial Day Massacre is a Chicago event that belongs in every account of American labor.

By 1941 union membership had roughly tripled since 1933, and the CIO's steel and auto unions were among the strongest institutions in working-class America. Unions raised wages, shortened hours and built the middle class of the postwar decades. Employers argued that they also raised costs and slowed change. The right to bargain collectively, and the limits on it, remain live questions in Illinois today, from teachers to warehouse workers.

lessons.title: Roosevelt and the Court
lessons.mainIdea: After the Supreme Court struck down key New Deal laws, Roosevelt tried to add justices, lost the fight, and yet won the Court.
reading: The Constitution gives judges the last word on whether a law is allowed, and in 1935 and 1936 the Supreme Court used it. It struck down the National Recovery Administration, unanimously, ruling that Congress had handed lawmaking power to industry codes and had reached into local business the Constitution left to the states. It struck down the farm program too. The justices, most of them appointed by earlier Republican presidents, read federal power narrowly, as courts had for decades. Roosevelt believed they would strike down Social Security and the Wagner Act next.

Fresh from a landslide re-election in 1936, he proposed in February 1937 to let the president appoint an extra justice for every justice over seventy who did not retire, up to six new seats. He said it would help elderly judges with their workload. Everyone understood the real purpose: to *pack the Court* with judges who would uphold the New Deal. The reaction shocked him. Newspapers, Republicans and many Democrats called it an attack on the independence of the courts and on the separation of powers. His own vice president opposed it. The bill died in the Senate that summer.

And yet Roosevelt got most of what he wanted. In the spring of 1937, while the fight raged, one justice began voting with the liberal side, and the Court upheld a state minimum wage law, the Wagner Act and then Social Security. Whether the justice switched because of the pressure is still argued; some evidence shows he had shifted before the plan was announced. Over the next four years retirements let Roosevelt appoint seven justices. The Court that emerged accepted broad federal power over the economy, a reading that held for the rest of the century.

The episode is a lesson in *checks and balances*. The Court checked the president and Congress. Congress and public opinion checked the president when he tried to bend the Court. And elections, over time, reshaped the Court anyway. Proposals to change the size of the Supreme Court have come back in recent years from both parties. The 1937 fight is the precedent everyone cites, and it is worth knowing what actually happened.

the power of courts to strike down laws that conflict with the Constitution
the way each branch of government can limit the others

lessons.title: The Argument That Never Ended
lessons.mainIdea: The New Deal did not end the Depression, but it permanently changed what Americans expect government to do, and the debate over that role continues.
reading: Did the New Deal work? Judge it by the numbers and the answer is mixed. Unemployment fell from about twenty-five percent in 1933 to about fourteen percent in 1937, then jumped again when Roosevelt cut spending to balance the budget. Full employment came only with World War II, when the government spent on ships and planes at a scale that dwarfed anything in the 1930s. Some economists say this proves that spending works and the New Deal was simply too small. Others say it proves that private investment, not government, creates lasting recovery. The same evidence supports two arguments.

Judge it by what it built and the answer is clearer. Deposit insurance, Social Security, unemployment insurance, the minimum wage, the right to unionize, rules for the stock market, rural electricity and thousands of schools and bridges all date from these years. Before 1933 the federal government touched most people's lives through the post office. After 1941 it was in their paycheck, their bank and their old age. Americans came to expect that Washington would act when the economy failed. That expectation itself is the New Deal's largest legacy.

The debate over the *role of government* has never closed. One side argues that markets, left alone, correct themselves and that government programs cost more than they deliver, create dependence and pile up debt for the next generation. The other argues that markets can fail catastrophically, that individuals cannot insure themselves against a whole economy collapsing, and that a democracy has both the power and the duty to protect its people. Each side has strong evidence from the 1930s, and each has weaknesses it prefers not to discuss.

You will meet this argument again in 2008, when banks collapsed and the government spent hundreds of billions to stop the fall. It returned in 2020, when a pandemic shut the economy and Congress sent checks to nearly every household. The people arguing then were, knowingly or not, arguing about the New Deal. Knowing what actually happened in the 1930s is the best equipment for judging the next version. What was tried? What worked? What did not?

chapters.title: World War II
chapters.bigQuestion: What did it take to win the Second World War, and what did the United States become in winning it?

story.title: The Squash Court Under the Stands
story.kicker: On a cold afternoon in December 1942, in a disused squash court beneath the football stands of the University of Chicago, forty-nine people watched the atomic age begin.
paragraphs: Stagg Field on the South Side of Chicago had not hosted a big game in years. Under its west stands, behind a locked door, was an old squash court with a concrete floor. Through the fall of 1942 a team led by the Italian physicist Enrico Fermi had been stacking graphite bricks there, layer on layer, with lumps of uranium set into them. The pile grew to a rough black sphere the size of a two-story house. They called it Chicago Pile-1. No one on the university's board had been told exactly what was being built under the stadium.

The idea was simple to state and terrifying to test. When a uranium atom splits, it throws out neutrons. If those neutrons hit other uranium atoms and split them too, you get a *chain reaction*. Slow it with graphite and control it with rods of cadmium that soak up neutrons, and you have a steady source of energy. Let it run wild and you have a bomb. Fermi's job was to prove that a controlled chain reaction could actually be made to happen. If his calculations were wrong, the pile could run away in a room in the middle of a city of three million people.

On Wednesday, December 2, 1942, the team gathered on a balcony overlooking the pile. Fermi ordered the control rods pulled out a few inches at a time. Counters clicked faster with each step. At each stage he checked his slide rule against the readings and called out what the next step should show. Around 3:25 in the afternoon he ordered the last rod withdrawn, and the clicking rose to a steady roar. The reaction was sustaining itself. After about four and a half minutes, Fermi ordered the rods pushed back in, and the counters slowed. Someone opened a bottle of wine and poured it into paper cups.

One of the leaders telephoned a colleague in Washington with a coded message: the Italian navigator had landed in the new world. The natives, he added, were friendly. Within three years the work begun under those stands had become the Manhattan Project, a secret effort employing well over a hundred thousand people in cities that did not appear on any map. In August 1945 it ended the war with two bombs that killed well over a hundred thousand people in Hiroshima and Nagasaki.

This chapter is about that war: how a country that wanted to stay out of it came to fight on two oceans, what it asked of the people at home, whom it locked up, whom it failed to save, and what it became by winning. The squash court is a good place to start, because everything about the war is in it: brilliance, secrecy, fear, and a decision whose consequences no one at that balcony could see.
story.think: Fermi ran the experiment in a crowded city because the war made waiting impossible. When, if ever, does urgency justify a risk that would be unacceptable in peacetime?

lessons.title: Staying Out
lessons.mainIdea: Most Americans in the 1930s wanted no part of another European war, and Congress wrote that wish into law until Roosevelt found ways around it.
reading: In 1934 a Senate committee spent months investigating why the United States had entered World War I. Its conclusion, that bankers and arms makers had pushed the country toward war for profit, was too simple, but millions believed it. More than a hundred thousand Americans had died in a war that seemed to have settled nothing. Between 1935 and 1937 Congress passed a series of *Neutrality Acts* that banned selling arms or lending money to any country at war. The idea was that if the United States sold nothing and owed nothing, it could not be dragged in again.

Meanwhile the world was coming apart. Japan invaded China in 1937. Adolf Hitler, who had taken power in Germany in 1933, took Austria in 1938 and Czechoslovakia in 1939. On September 1, 1939, Germany invaded Poland, and Britain and France declared war. By June 1940 France had fallen and Britain stood alone, bombed nightly. Roosevelt believed the United States could not stay out, but a large *isolationist* movement, led by figures like the aviator Charles Lindbergh and strong in the Midwest, argued that America should defend its own hemisphere and nothing more. The Chicago Tribune was the movement's loudest newspaper.

Roosevelt moved step by step. In 1940 he traded fifty old destroyers to Britain for naval bases and pushed through the first peacetime draft in American history. In March 1941 Congress passed *Lend-Lease*, which let the president lend weapons and supplies to any country whose defense he judged vital to the United States. Roosevelt compared it to lending a garden hose to a neighbor whose house was on fire. Over the war Lend-Lease sent about fifty billion dollars in aid, mostly to Britain and the Soviet Union. By the fall of 1941 American warships were escorting convoys and being fired on by German submarines.

In a January 1941 speech Roosevelt described a world worth fighting for, one built on four freedoms: of speech, of worship, from want and from fear. He was preparing the country for a war it had not yet entered. Historians debate how far he led public opinion and how far he followed it. What is clear is that in November 1941 most Americans still hoped to stay out, and one Sunday morning ended that hope.

someone who believes the United States should stay out of other countries' wars
the 1941 law that let the president lend weapons and supplies to countries fighting the Axis

lessons.title: Pearl Harbor
lessons.mainIdea: Japan's surprise attack on December 7, 1941, ended the debate over neutrality in a single morning and brought the United States into a global war.
reading: Japan and the United States had been on a collision course for years. Japan's leaders wanted an empire in East Asia and the oil, rubber and metals of Southeast Asia. The United States, which supplied most of Japan's oil, cut off those shipments in the summer of 1941 to force Japan out of China. Japan's military decided that if it was going to seize the oil of the Dutch East Indies it had to first cripple the American fleet based at *Pearl Harbor*, Hawaii. Talks in Washington continued while a fleet of six aircraft carriers steamed east in silence.

Just before eight on Sunday morning, December 7, 1941, the first wave of about one hundred eighty Japanese planes came over the mountains of Oahu. The American battleships were moored in a row. Within two hours, the attackers had sunk or badly damaged eight battleships and destroyed most of the aircraft on the island's airfields. About twenty-four hundred Americans were killed, nearly half of them on the battleship Arizona, which exploded and sank with more than a thousand men aboard. Japan lost twenty-nine planes. By luck, the American carriers were at sea and untouched.

The next day Roosevelt asked Congress to declare war, calling December 7 a date which will live in infamy. The vote was nearly unanimous. Three days later Germany and Italy, Japan's allies, declared war on the United States. The isolationist movement dissolved overnight; Lindbergh asked to fly combat missions. The country that had argued for two years about whether to fight was now at war on two oceans against three powers, with an army smaller than Portugal's had been a few years earlier.

Pearl Harbor also raised questions that historians still study. Why was the fleet caught by surprise when American code-breakers were reading Japanese diplomatic messages? The answer, most conclude, was not conspiracy but ordinary failure: warnings that were vague, sent too slowly or read by the wrong people. The attack taught a lesson that shaped American policy for the rest of the century. Never again, leaders decided, would the country be unprepared or wait for the enemy to strike first.

lessons.title: Arsenal of Democracy
lessons.mainIdea: The war ended the Depression by turning the whole economy toward production, and the federal government directed it.
reading: The United States won the war partly with a weapon no other country could match: its factories. In 1939 American plants built a few thousand military aircraft. By 1944 they built almost a hundred thousand in a single year. Ford built a plant at Willow Run, Michigan, that turned out a four-engine bomber roughly every hour. Shipyards on the West Coast launched cargo ships in weeks instead of months. By the end of the war the United States had produced more weapons than all the Axis countries combined. Roosevelt called it the arsenal of democracy.

This did not happen by itself. The War Production Board, a federal agency, told companies what to make and what they could not make. No new cars were built for civilians from early 1942 until the war ended; the auto plants built tanks and planes. The government set prices, froze many wages and rationed scarce goods. Every family got *ration* books with stamps for sugar, coffee, meat, gasoline and shoes. Drivers had a sticker on the windshield showing how much gas they could buy. Americans grew vegetables in victory gardens and collected scrap metal and cooking fat for the war.

The war was paid for two ways. Taxes rose sharply, and for the first time most working Americans paid federal income tax, taken out of their paychecks. The rest was borrowed by selling *war bonds* to the public, with movie stars and schoolchildren leading the drives. Federal spending rose to about ninety billion dollars a year, ten times the level of the late 1930s. The Depression simply ended. Unemployment fell below two percent. Wages rose, and with little to buy, families saved.

The war also moved people. Millions left farms and small towns for jobs in Detroit, Los Angeles, Seattle and Chicago, which became a center of aircraft engine and munitions production. Hundreds of thousands of Black southerners came north in a second Great Migration. Mexican workers came under a program called the *bracero* agreement to fill farm jobs. Crowded cities, housing shortages and racial tension followed; in Detroit in 1943 a riot killed thirty-four people. The home front was not always united.

lessons.title: Women and War Work
lessons.mainIdea: With millions of men in uniform, women took factory jobs once closed to them, and the war changed ideas about women's work even though most were pushed out when it ended.
reading: About sixteen million Americans served in the armed forces during the war. Someone had to build the planes. Between 1940 and 1945 the number of women in paid work rose by roughly six million, to about nineteen million, and for the first time married women and mothers went to work in large numbers. They welded ship hulls, riveted bomber wings and ran drill presses. The government and the press celebrated the figure of Rosie the Riveter, a strong woman in coveralls with her sleeves rolled up. Posters told women that they could do it.

The reality was more complicated than the poster. Women were usually paid less than the men they replaced. Many employers hired them reluctantly and expected them to leave the moment the war ended. Child care was scarce; the government funded some centers, but most working mothers relied on relatives. Black women, who had mostly been limited to domestic work, fought for and won factory jobs, often in the least pleasant departments. Still, the paycheck and the skill were real. Many women said later that the war was the first time anyone had treated them as capable of serious work.

Women also served in uniform. About three hundred fifty thousand joined the women's branches of the Army, Navy, Coast Guard and Marines, mostly as clerks, mechanics, nurses and radio operators. About a thousand women flew military planes as ferry pilots and trainers in the *WASP* program, delivering aircraft from factories to bases so male pilots could go to combat. Thirty-eight of them died. They were considered civilians and were not granted veteran status until 1977.

When the war ended, the factories laid women off first to make room for returning soldiers, and government messages switched to urging women home. Most of the gains in factory work vanished within two years. Yet the share of women working never fell back to prewar levels, and the daughters of the Rosies grew up knowing what their mothers had done. Historians see the war less as a revolution than as a crack in the wall, one that the women's movement of the 1960s would widen.

lessons.title: Japanese American Incarceration
lessons.mainIdea: In 1942 the government removed about one hundred twenty thousand people of Japanese ancestry, most of them citizens, from the West Coast and held them in camps without charges.
reading: After Pearl Harbor, fear and old racism toward Asians on the West Coast combined into demands for action. Newspapers, politicians and some generals claimed that Japanese Americans might help an invasion, though no evidence of sabotage was ever found. On February 19, 1942, Roosevelt signed *Executive Order 9066*, which let the Army declare military zones and remove anyone from them. The Army used it against one group only. About one hundred twenty thousand people of Japanese ancestry living in California, Oregon, Washington and Arizona were ordered out. About two-thirds were American citizens by birth.

Families were given days, sometimes a week, to settle their affairs. They could take only what they could carry. Farms, shops and homes were sold for a fraction of their value or simply lost. People were first held at racetracks and fairgrounds, sleeping in horse stalls, then moved to ten camps in remote deserts and swamps from California to Arkansas. The camps had barbed wire, guard towers and barracks with no privacy. Schools, newspapers and baseball leagues sprang up inside, run by the prisoners themselves. Most stayed for about three years.

The government called it evacuation and relocation. The people inside, and most historians now, call it *incarceration*: imprisonment without charge or trial. In 1944 the Supreme Court upheld the removal in Korematsu v. United States, ruling that military necessity in wartime justified it. Three justices dissented. One wrote that the order fell into the ugly abyss of racism. Another warned that the ruling was a loaded weapon that any future government could pick up. Decades later the government admitted that the Army's claim of necessity had rested on false statements.

Meanwhile thousands of young men from the camps volunteered for the Army. The 442nd Regimental Combat Team, made up of Japanese Americans, fought in Italy and France and became one of the most decorated units of its size in American history. In 1988 Congress formally apologized and paid twenty thousand dollars to each surviving prisoner. The episode is studied as a test of what the Constitution means when a frightened country decides that one group is the enemy.

lessons.title: Europe: From North Africa to D-Day
lessons.mainIdea: The Allies defeated Germany by wearing it down on the Eastern Front, bombing it from the air and landing in France on June 6, 1944.
reading: The Allies agreed that Germany, not Japan, was the greater danger and had to be beaten first. But the biggest share of the fighting in Europe was done by the Soviet Union, which Germany had invaded in June 1941. On the Eastern Front, millions of soldiers fought along a line a thousand miles long. At Stalingrad, in the winter of 1942 to 1943, the Soviets surrounded and destroyed an entire German army. Roughly eight of every ten German soldiers who died in the war died fighting the Soviets. Stalin demanded that the Americans and British open a second front in France, and for two years they were not ready.

Instead the western Allies started at the edges. American troops landed in North Africa in November 1942 and, after early defeats, learned how to fight. They took Sicily in 1943 and pushed slowly up Italy against fierce resistance. Meanwhile American and British bombers attacked German cities and factories day and night. The bombing killed hundreds of thousands of civilians, and historians still debate how much it shortened the war. It did force Germany to pull fighters and guns back from the front to defend its cities.

The second front finally opened on June 6, 1944: *D-Day*. Under General Dwight Eisenhower, about one hundred fifty-six thousand American, British and Canadian troops crossed the English Channel and landed on five beaches in Normandy, France, in the largest seaborne invasion in history. At Omaha Beach, Americans came ashore under machine-gun fire from cliffs and took thousands of casualties in a single morning. By nightfall all five beaches were held. Within weeks a million Allied soldiers were in France. Paris was freed in August.

Germany struck back once, in December 1944, through the forests of Belgium in the Battle of the Bulge, the largest battle the U.S. Army fought in the war. American troops held, at a cost of about nineteen thousand killed. In the spring of 1945 the Allies crossed the Rhine from the west while the Soviets fought into Berlin from the east. Hitler killed himself on April 30. Germany surrendered on May 8, 1945, celebrated as V-E Day, victory in Europe.

lessons.title: The Pacific: Island by Island
lessons.mainIdea: After turning the tide at Midway, the United States fought across the Pacific island by island in a brutal campaign that made an invasion of Japan look unbearable.
reading: For six months after Pearl Harbor, Japan won everywhere. It took the Philippines, where about seventy-five thousand American and Filipino prisoners were marched sixty-five miles with little food or water in the Bataan Death March, and thousands died. It took Singapore, the Dutch East Indies and islands across the Pacific. Then in June 1942 the Japanese navy tried to seize the tiny American base at *Midway*. American code-breakers had read the plan. In a single day American carrier planes sank four Japanese aircraft carriers. Japan never recovered the initiative.

The Pacific war was fought over water on a scale hard to imagine, and it was fought for islands, some no more than a mile long, that could hold an airfield. The American strategy was *island hopping*: seize the islands that mattered, bypass the rest and let their garrisons starve. Guadalcanal, Tarawa, Saipan, Iwo Jima, Okinawa. Each landing meant Marines wading ashore into gunfire from bunkers dug into coral and volcanic rock. Japanese soldiers were ordered never to surrender, and almost none did. On Iwo Jima in early 1945, about seven thousand Americans died to take eight square miles.

The fighting was marked by hatred on both sides that historians have called a war without mercy. Japanese forces committed atrocities against prisoners and civilians across Asia. American propaganda showed the Japanese as animals, and some American troops killed prisoners and took body parts as trophies. Meanwhile Navajo Marines used their own language as an unbreakable code, and Black units and Mexican American soldiers fought in a military that was still segregated.

Okinawa, from April to June 1945, was the worst. About twelve thousand Americans died, along with roughly a hundred thousand Japanese soldiers and a similar number of Okinawan civilians, many of whom were forced or persuaded to kill themselves rather than surrender. Japanese *kamikaze* pilots deliberately crashed planes into American ships. Planners looking at an invasion of Japan itself, scheduled for November 1945, expected casualties far beyond anything yet seen. That expectation shaped the decision you will read about in the next section.

lessons.title: The Holocaust and America's Response
lessons.mainIdea: Nazi Germany murdered six million Jews and millions of others, and the United States, which knew much of what was happening, did little to rescue them until late in the war.
reading: From the moment Hitler took power in 1933 the Nazi government stripped German Jews of their rights, their jobs and their property. After the war began, Germany's conquests placed millions more Jews under its control. Beginning in 1941, special units shot Jews by the hundreds of thousands in Eastern Europe, and in 1942 Germany built camps designed for killing. At Auschwitz and five other death camps in occupied Poland, trains arrived daily and most passengers were murdered in gas chambers within hours. By 1945 about six million Jews had been killed, along with millions of others: Poles, Soviet prisoners, Roma, disabled people, and gay men. We call this the *Holocaust*.

How much did Americans know? A great deal, and earlier than many later claimed. Reports of mass shootings reached newspapers in 1941 and 1942. In late 1942 the State Department confirmed a report that Germany planned to kill all the Jews of Europe, and the Allies publicly condemned it. But the news was often buried on inside pages, and many readers found it hard to believe. Before the war, the strict immigration quotas of 1924 kept most Jewish refugees out. In 1939 the ship St. Louis, carrying more than nine hundred Jewish refugees, was turned away from the United States and returned to Europe, where about a quarter of its passengers were later murdered.

The official position was that the fastest way to save the Jews was to win the war. Requests to bomb the rail lines to Auschwitz were refused as a diversion of resources, even though American bombers hit factories a few miles away in 1944. Officials in the State Department delayed rescue proposals and, in some cases, hid information. Only in January 1944, after Treasury officials documented that delay in a report to the president, did Roosevelt create the War Refugee Board. It helped save perhaps two hundred thousand people, largely in Hungary, proof of what earlier action might have done.

In April 1945 American troops reached camps like Ohrdruf, Buchenwald and Dachau and found the dead and the dying. General Eisenhower ordered soldiers, reporters and members of Congress to see it so that no one could later claim it had not happened. The Holocaust is studied as the extreme case of what a modern state can do, and America's response as a lesson about what a democracy owes to strangers in danger. The questions it raises are still argued whenever refugees ask for shelter.

lessons.title: The Manhattan Project
lessons.mainIdea: Fearing a German bomb, the United States built a secret atomic weapon in three years, and Chicago was where the key experiment happened.
reading: In 1939 scientists who had fled Nazi Germany learned that German physicists had split the uranium atom. Albert Einstein signed a letter to Roosevelt warning that Germany might build a bomb of unimaginable power. Roosevelt started a small research program. After Pearl Harbor it became the *Manhattan Project*, run by the Army under General Leslie Groves with the physicist J. Robert Oppenheimer leading the weapons laboratory. It would cost about two billion dollars, employ well over a hundred thousand people, and remain secret from nearly all of them. Most workers never knew what they were building.

Chicago's role came first. Fermi's pile under Stagg Field proved on December 2, 1942, that a controlled chain reaction was possible. That was the foundation for everything else. Huge plants were built in secret at Oak Ridge, Tennessee, to separate the rare kind of uranium that could be used in a bomb, and at Hanford, Washington, where giant reactors modeled on Fermi's pile produced a new element, *plutonium*. At Los Alamos, New Mexico, scientists designed the bombs themselves. Vice President Harry Truman, who had chaired a Senate committee on war spending, was told nothing until he became president in April 1945.

On July 16, 1945, in the desert of New Mexico, the first atomic bomb was tested. The explosion was brighter than the sun, and the blast was felt more than a hundred miles away. Oppenheimer later said a line from Hindu scripture had come to him: he had become death, the destroyer of worlds. Germany, the original reason for the project, had surrendered two months earlier and had never come close to a bomb. The weapon would now be used, if at all, against Japan.

Some of the Chicago scientists objected. In June 1945 a group led by James Franck sent a report arguing that using the bomb on a city without warning would start an arms race with the Soviet Union and cost the United States the world's trust. They proposed a demonstration on an empty island instead. Their report was set aside. A generation later some of the same scientists founded a magazine in Chicago whose cover carries a clock showing how close the world stands to catastrophe, a warning that has never been retired.

lessons.title: Hiroshima and Nagasaki
lessons.mainIdea: Two atomic bombs in August 1945 killed well over a hundred thousand people and ended the war, and the decision to use them is still debated on the evidence.
reading: On August 6, 1945, a single American plane dropped a uranium bomb on the city of Hiroshima. The blast, the heat and the fires destroyed most of the city in seconds. About seventy thousand people died that day, and tens of thousands more died from injuries and radiation sickness by the end of the year; the total is usually given as more than a hundred thousand. On August 9 a plutonium bomb fell on Nagasaki and killed at least forty thousand more. On the same day the Soviet Union, keeping a promise to the Allies, declared war on Japan and attacked its army in Manchuria.

On August 15 Japan's emperor announced surrender by radio, the first time most Japanese had heard his voice. The formal surrender was signed on an American battleship in Tokyo Bay on September 2, 1945. The war was over. In the United States the news brought crowds into the streets. Most Americans, and most soldiers waiting to invade Japan, believed the bomb had saved their lives, and polls at the time showed overwhelming approval.

Historians have argued ever since, and the argument turns on evidence. The case for the decision: Japan's leaders had rejected surrender demands, Okinawa showed what an invasion would cost, and even after Hiroshima the Japanese cabinet was deadlocked until the emperor intervened. The case against: Japan was already blockaded and starving, some Japanese leaders had been seeking peace through the Soviets, the United States refused to say whether the emperor could stay, and the Soviet attack may have mattered as much as the bombs. Some historians add that Truman also wanted to impress the Soviet Union. There is evidence for each claim, and no document settles it.

What is not in doubt is what the bombs did. The survivors, called *hibakusha* in Japanese, suffered burns, cancers and stigma for the rest of their lives, and many of them spent those lives telling the world what they had seen. The United States has never used a nuclear weapon since, and neither has anyone else, but nine countries now have them. The question the Chicago scientists asked in June 1945 became the central question of the next fifty years.

Japanese word for the survivors of the atomic bombings
giving up with no terms or promises from the winning side
illness caused by exposure to the invisible energy released by a nuclear explosion

look.text: In a statement released from the White House, Truman announced that an American plane had dropped one bomb on Hiroshima with more power than twenty thousand tons of TNT. He said it was an atomic bomb, a harnessing of the basic power of the universe, and warned that if Japan did not surrender, it could expect a rain of ruin from the air.

lessons.title: A New World and the GI Bill
lessons.mainIdea: The war left the United States the richest and most powerful nation on earth, committed to a new United Nations and to sending millions of veterans to college.
reading: When the shooting stopped, the world had changed shape. Britain and France were exhausted. Germany and Japan lay in ruins under occupation. China was sliding into civil war. Only two countries came out stronger: the Soviet Union, with the largest army in the world and control of Eastern Europe, and the United States, whose factories were untouched and whose economy produced about half of everything made on earth. The United States alone had the atomic bomb. These two powers, allies for four years, would soon be enemies for forty.

Roosevelt had died in April 1945, but his plan for the peace went forward. In June 1945 fifty countries met in San Francisco to sign the charter of the *United Nations*, an organization meant to succeed where the League of Nations had failed after World War I. Its Security Council gave the five main victors, including the United States and the Soviet Union, a veto over its actions. Unlike 1919, the Senate approved American membership overwhelmingly. Trials at Nuremberg put surviving Nazi leaders before an international court for war crimes and crimes against humanity, setting a precedent that still shapes international law.

At home, Congress had planned ahead. The Servicemen's Readjustment Act of 1944, known as the *GI Bill*, offered every returning veteran money for college or job training, low-interest loans to buy a home or start a business, and a year of unemployment pay. About eight million veterans used the education benefit. Colleges that had served the wealthy filled with the sons of factory workers and farmers. Home loans built the suburbs. Economists count the GI Bill among the best investments the government ever made.

The bill's promise was not equal. It was administered locally, and in the South, and often in the North, Black veterans were steered away from colleges, denied loans by banks and shut out of new suburbs by rules that barred Black buyers. About a million Black Americans had served. Their exclusion from much of the GI Bill's wealth is one root of the gap in family wealth that persists today. The war made the United States a superpower and built its middle class, and it left the question of who belonged to that middle class for the next generation to fight over.

the 1944 law giving veterans money for college, home loans and unemployment pay
a nation with enough military and economic strength to shape events worldwide
the trials of Nazi leaders after the war for war crimes and crimes against humanity

chapters.title: The Cold War at Home and Abroad
chapters.bigQuestion: How did a war that was never declared shape American life for nearly thirty years?

story.title: Thirteen Days
story.kicker: In October 1962 a set of photographs taken from seventy thousand feet put two nuclear powers closer to war than they have ever been, before or since.
paragraphs: Tuesday, October 16, 1962, 8:45 in the morning. President John F. Kennedy is still in his bedroom at the White House when his national security adviser brings in the photographs. They were taken two days earlier by a U-2 spy plane flying high over western Cuba. Analysts have circled long shapes on trailers, tents and construction crews. They are Soviet medium-range nuclear missiles, ninety miles from Florida, and within days they could reach Washington in minutes. The Soviet leader, Nikita Khrushchev, has been promising all summer that no offensive weapons would go to Cuba.

For six days, in secret, Kennedy and a dozen advisers argue in the Cabinet Room. The generals want an air strike followed by an invasion. Others warn that an attack could kill Soviet troops and start a war that would end with nuclear weapons falling on American cities. Kennedy has recently read a history of how Europe's leaders blundered into World War I in 1914, one step at a time, and he says he does not intend to write that book's sequel. By the weekend he has chosen a middle course: a naval blockade, which he calls a quarantine, to stop more missiles arriving, plus a demand that the ones already there be removed.

Monday, October 22, 7:00 in the evening. Kennedy goes on television and tells the country, and the world, what the photographs show. Any missile launched from Cuba, he says, will be treated as an attack by the Soviet Union on the United States. American forces go to the highest state of alert short of war. Bombers with nuclear weapons stay in the air around the clock. In Chicago and every other city, families stock canned food and children practice crouching under desks. On Wednesday Soviet ships approach the quarantine line, slow, and turn back.

Saturday, October 27, the worst day. A U-2 is shot down over Cuba and its pilot killed. Another U-2 strays into Soviet airspace over Alaska by mistake. Two letters arrive from Khrushchev, one conciliatory and one demanding that American missiles in Turkey be removed too. Kennedy answers the first letter publicly and ignores the second. That night his brother Robert meets the Soviet ambassador in secret and promises that the missiles in Turkey will quietly go within a few months, so long as no one says the two are connected.

Sunday morning, October 28, Radio Moscow announces that the missiles will be dismantled and shipped home. The crisis ends. Only decades later did the world learn how close it had come: Soviet submarines near the quarantine line carried nuclear torpedoes, and Soviet troops in Cuba had short-range nuclear weapons that an invasion would have met. Both leaders had bargained in secret while speaking in public, and the secret bargain is what kept the peace. This chapter is about the world that could produce such a week.
story.think: Kennedy hid the missile trade from the public and even from most of his advisers. Was that secrecy justified? What does the episode suggest about how much citizens can know about decisions made in their name?

lessons.title: The Truman Doctrine and the Marshall Plan
lessons.mainIdea: Facing Soviet control of Eastern Europe, the United States adopted containment: using money and commitments to stop communism from spreading further.
reading: The wartime alliance broke apart within two years of victory. The Soviet Union had lost more than twenty million people to a German invasion and wanted friendly governments on its borders. By 1947 it had installed Communist regimes across Eastern Europe, and Winston Churchill said an iron curtain had fallen across the continent. American leaders saw a dictatorship expanding as Hitler's had. Soviet leaders saw a rich rival with the atomic bomb building bases around them. Each side read the other's defense as aggression. This standoff, fought with money, spies, weapons and words but never directly with armies, is called the *Cold War*.

The American strategy took its name from a diplomat named George Kennan. Writing from Moscow in 1946, he argued that Soviet power could not be talked out of expanding but could be *contained*: blocked firmly wherever it pushed, until the Soviet system changed or collapsed from within. In March 1947 President Harry Truman asked Congress for four hundred million dollars to help Greece, where Communists were fighting a civil war, and Turkey, which the Soviets were pressuring. The principle he announced, that the United States would support free peoples resisting takeover, became the *Truman Doctrine*. It committed the country to a global role it had rejected in 1919.

Western Europe was still in ruins, and hunger and unemployment were feeding Communist parties in France and Italy. In 1948 Congress approved Secretary of State George Marshall's plan to send about thirteen billion dollars in aid to rebuild European economies. The *Marshall Plan* was offered to the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe too, but Stalin refused and forced his satellites to refuse. Within four years Western European production was above prewar levels. Historians count it among the most successful foreign policies in American history, and note that it also created customers for American goods.

Not everyone agreed. Some conservatives argued that the country could not afford to rebuild the world. Some on the left, including Roosevelt's former vice president Henry Wallace, argued that the tough line was provoking a conflict that could have been avoided. Historians still debate who started the Cold War, and the answer depends partly on which archives you read; Soviet documents opened after 1991 changed several arguments. What is clear is that by 1948 both sides believed the other would seize any opening.

words.d: the rivalry between the United States and the Soviet Union from about 1947 to 1991, fought without direct war between them
the American strategy of blocking Soviet expansion wherever it pushed
Truman's 1947 pledge to support free peoples resisting takeover by armed minorities or outside pressure
the American program of about thirteen billion dollars to rebuild Western Europe after 1948
