lessons.title: Berlin, NATO and the Bomb
lessons.mainIdea: The Berlin airlift, the NATO alliance and the Soviet atomic bomb in 1949 turned the Cold War into a permanent, armed standoff.
reading: Berlin lay a hundred miles inside the Soviet zone of occupied Germany, divided among the four Allied powers. In June 1948, angry that the western Allies were creating a separate West German state, Stalin cut every road and rail line into the western sectors of the city. Two million people faced starvation or surrender. Truman refused to give up the city and refused to shoot his way in. Instead, for eleven months, American and British planes landed in West Berlin around the clock, one every few minutes, carrying coal, flour and milk. The *Berlin airlift* delivered more than two million tons. In May 1949 Stalin lifted the blockade.

The crisis convinced Western Europe and the United States to bind themselves together. In April 1949 twelve countries signed the North Atlantic Treaty, creating *NATO*. Its core promise is that an attack on any member is an attack on all. For the first time in its history, the United States joined a permanent military alliance in peacetime and stationed troops in Europe to stay. The Soviet Union answered with its own alliance, the Warsaw Pact, in 1955. Germany itself was split into two countries, and in 1961 the East German government built a wall through Berlin to stop its people fleeing west.

Then two shocks in the fall of 1949. In August the Soviet Union tested its own atomic bomb, years before American experts had expected. In October Mao Zedong's Communists won the civil war in China, the world's most populous country. To many Americans it seemed that communism was winning everywhere and that spies must be to blame. Truman ordered a crash program to build the hydrogen bomb, a weapon hundreds of times more powerful than the one dropped on Hiroshima, and a secret planning document called for a huge increase in military spending to meet a global threat.

By the mid-1950s both sides had hydrogen bombs and were building missiles to deliver them across oceans. Each could destroy the other within an hour, and neither could stop an attack. Strategists called this *mutual assured destruction*: peace kept by the certainty that any war would kill everyone. Schoolchildren practiced duck-and-cover drills. Families in the Chicago suburbs dug backyard shelters. The arms race would consume trillions of dollars and shape science, schools and politics for a generation.

the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, the 1949 alliance in which an attack on one member counts as an attack on all
a competition between nations to build more and better weapons
the idea that neither side will start a nuclear war because both would be destroyed

check.why: Peace rested on the certainty that any nuclear war would kill everyone on both sides.

lessons.title: Korea
lessons.mainIdea: The Korean War of 1950 to 1953 was the first shooting war of containment; it cost about thirty-six thousand American lives and ended where it began.
reading: Korea had been divided at the end of World War II along the thirty-eighth parallel, with a Soviet-backed Communist state in the north and an American-backed state in the south. On June 25, 1950, North Korean troops with Soviet tanks poured across the line and nearly overran the whole peninsula. Truman decided within days that this was the test of containment. He sent American forces under the flag of the United Nations, which the Soviets had been boycotting and so could not veto. He never asked Congress for a declaration of war, calling it a police action, a precedent every president since has used.

In September General Douglas MacArthur landed troops far behind North Korean lines at Inchon, a brilliant gamble that collapsed the invasion. American and UN forces chased the North Koreans back across the parallel and drove toward the Chinese border, aiming now to unite Korea. In November, hundreds of thousands of Chinese soldiers crossed the border and sent the Americans into the longest retreat in their history through a brutal winter. When MacArthur publicly demanded permission to attack China itself, Truman fired him in April 1951 for defying civilian control of the military. Many Americans were furious, but the principle held.

For two more years the war settled into trench fighting near the thirty-eighth parallel while negotiators argued, mostly over prisoners who did not want to go home. An *armistice* signed in July 1953 stopped the shooting but never became a peace treaty; the two Koreas remain technically at war, separated by the most heavily armed border on earth, with American troops still stationed in the south. About thirty-six thousand Americans died. Korean deaths, civilian and military, on both sides, are estimated in the millions.

Korea set the pattern for the Cold War. It was a *limited war*: fought for limited goals, without nuclear weapons, in a place most Americans could not find on a map, and ended by negotiation rather than victory. It tripled the American defense budget and left the country with bases across Asia. It also showed how the Cold War could turn hot far from either superpower, with the people who lived there paying most of the price. Americans often call it the forgotten war, which tells you something about how nations remember wars that end in a draw.

an agreement to stop fighting that is not a full peace treaty
a war fought for limited goals without using all available weapons
the principle that elected leaders, not generals, make the final military decisions

lessons.title: McCarthyism
lessons.mainIdea: Fear of Communist spies fed a wave of investigations and blacklists that ruined thousands of careers, until Senator McCarthy overreached on television.
reading: There were real Soviet spies in the United States. Klaus Fuchs, a scientist at Los Alamos, gave the Soviets bomb secrets, and Julius Rosenberg ran a spy ring; he and his wife Ethel were executed in 1953. But the search for spies grew into something much larger. In 1947 Truman ordered loyalty checks for every federal employee. The House Un-American Activities Committee investigated Hollywood, and ten writers and directors who refused to answer went to prison. Studios kept a *blacklist* of people who would never work again. Teachers, union leaders and government workers lost jobs over meetings they had attended in the 1930s.

In February 1950 a little-known senator from Wisconsin, Joseph McCarthy, told an audience in West Virginia that he had a list of Communists working in the State Department. The number changed every time he spoke. He never produced the list. But the charge came days after the Soviet bomb and the fall of China, and it made him the most feared man in Washington. For four years he accused diplomats, professors, generals and journalists, usually with no evidence, and any senator who challenged him risked being called soft on communism. *McCarthyism* came to mean reckless accusation without proof.

The end came on television. In 1954 McCarthy took on the U.S. Army, and the hearings were broadcast live for weeks to about twenty million viewers. Americans watched him bully witnesses and interrupt everyone. When he attacked a young lawyer on the Army's legal team, the Army's counsel, Joseph Welch, asked him whether he had no sense of decency. The gallery applauded. In December the Senate formally condemned McCarthy's conduct. He died three years later, largely ignored. The broader fear faded more slowly, and the blacklists lasted into the 1960s.

The episode raises questions the Constitution does not answer cleanly. The government has a duty to catch spies. It also has a duty not to punish people for their beliefs or their associations. Where is the line? Later evidence from Soviet archives confirmed some of the espionage, and also confirmed that the vast majority of McCarthy's targets were innocent. Historians use the era to study how fear travels through a democracy and what stops it.

lessons.title: Suburbs, Babies and Highways
lessons.mainIdea: Postwar prosperity, cheap home loans and new highways moved millions of families to the suburbs, and left cities and Black families behind.
reading: Between 1946 and 1964 Americans had about seventy-six million babies, a *baby boom* that reshaped every school, store and neighborhood. Returning veterans married young and wanted houses that did not exist. A builder named William Levitt applied the assembly line to housing: crews moved down a street doing one task each, and a house went up in a day. His first Levittown on Long Island had seventeen thousand nearly identical homes. GI Bill and federal loans meant a veteran could buy one for almost nothing down, often for less per month than city rent. By 1960 a quarter of Americans lived in suburbs.

The car made the suburb possible, and the government made the car king. In 1956 President Eisenhower, who remembered a miserable Army convoy across the country in 1919 and the German autobahns in 1945, signed the Interstate Highway Act. It funded about forty-one thousand miles of limited-access highway, the largest public works project in American history, justified partly as a way to evacuate cities in a nuclear attack. Chicago's expressways date from these years. Highways carried families out of the city and shopping malls followed them. Towns bypassed by the interstate withered.

The suburbs were not open to everyone. Federal loan agencies refused to insure mortgages in neighborhoods they marked in red on their maps, mostly Black and mixed neighborhoods, a practice called *redlining*. Levitt's contracts barred sales to Black buyers, and when a Black family moved into a Levittown in 1957, mobs gathered for weeks. In Chicago, highways were routed through Black neighborhoods, and public housing towers concentrated poor families on the South and West Sides. The suburbs built white middle-class wealth in homes that gained value; Black families were largely locked out of that wealth.

Life in the new suburbs had its critics. Writers worried about conformity, about identical houses full of identical families watching identical television. Women who had worked during the war found themselves expected to stay home, and a 1963 book by Betty Friedan gave a name to their restlessness. Television itself, in almost no homes in 1948 and nearly ninety percent by 1960, became the country's shared culture. The teenagers of the boom, with money and cars, invented rock and roll audiences. The suburbs were prosperous and often happy, and they set up the conflicts of the next decade.

refusing loans or insurance in neighborhoods marked as risky, mostly Black neighborhoods
a limited-access highway in the national system funded by the 1956 act
behaving like everyone else rather than as an individual

lessons.title: The Space Race
lessons.mainIdea: A Soviet satellite in 1957 shocked the United States into a race for space that put Americans on the Moon twelve years later.
reading: On October 4, 1957, the Soviet Union launched *Sputnik*, a polished metal sphere the size of a beach ball that circled the earth every ninety-six minutes, beeping. Americans could hear it on the radio and, at dawn, see the rocket that carried it. The shock was enormous. The rocket that could lift a satellite could carry a hydrogen bomb to any American city. The country that had assumed it led the world in science had been beaten by a nation it thought backward. A month later the Soviets launched a dog into orbit. An American attempt in December rose four feet and exploded on live television.

The response reached into every classroom. Congress created *NASA* in 1958 and passed the National Defense Education Act, which poured money into science, math and foreign language teaching and into college loans; if you have taken a federal student loan, it began here. The Soviets kept winning. In April 1961 Yuri Gagarin became the first human in orbit. Three weeks later Alan Shepard made a fifteen-minute flight that did not reach orbit. President Kennedy, looking for a contest the United States could win, asked Congress in May 1961 to commit to landing a man on the Moon and returning him safely before the decade was out.

It was a staggering promise. No one knew how to do it. Over eight years NASA spent about twenty-five billion dollars, employed some four hundred thousand people, and lost three astronauts in a launch-pad fire in 1967. The program built rockets taller than the Statue of Liberty and computers small enough to fly. Much of the engineering was done by contractors in Texas, California and Florida, and much of the calculation, in the early years, by women mathematicians whose names were left out of the story for decades.

On July 20, 1969, Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin landed on the Moon while about six hundred million people watched on television, the largest audience in history to that point. Americans landed there six times in all. Critics then and since have asked whether the money could have been better spent on earth, and the Moon landings did not change the balance of the Cold War. But the race produced satellites for weather and communication, the computer industry, and a generation of scientists. It also produced a photograph of the earth from space, small and alone, that helped start the environmental movement.

lessons.title: After the Missile Crisis
lessons.mainIdea: The Cuban Missile Crisis frightened both superpowers into the first steps toward limiting nuclear weapons, even as the arms race continued.
reading: The story that opened this chapter did not come from nowhere. In 1959 Fidel Castro had overthrown a dictator in Cuba and, when the United States turned hostile, allied with the Soviet Union. In April 1961 Kennedy allowed an invasion by Cuban exiles trained by the CIA at the Bay of Pigs. It failed in three days, humiliating the new president. Khrushchev concluded that Kennedy was weak, and in 1962 he sent missiles to Cuba, partly to defend Castro and partly to offset the American lead in missiles and American weapons in Turkey. The photographs of October 14 found them.

The thirteen days changed both men. Kennedy had seen how close a chain of small decisions could come to catastrophe, and Khrushchev had seen the same. Within a year they installed a direct teletype link, the *hot line*, so leaders could talk in a crisis instead of guessing. In August 1963 they signed the Limited Test Ban Treaty, ending nuclear tests in the atmosphere, which had been spreading radioactive fallout across the globe, into milk and children's teeth. It was the first agreement of the nuclear age to restrain the weapons themselves.

Kennedy gave a speech in June 1963 asking Americans to re-examine their view of the Soviet Union and to remember that both peoples breathed the same air and cherished their children's future. Five months later he was assassinated in Dallas, on November 22, 1963. Khrushchev was removed by his own colleagues the next year, partly for the humiliation of Cuba. The arms race did not stop; both sides built thousands more missiles, and by the 1980s the world held tens of thousands of nuclear warheads. But the pattern of talking, testing limits and signing treaties began in the aftermath of October 1962.

Historians use the crisis to study how decisions get made under pressure. Tapes Kennedy secretly recorded in the Cabinet Room let us hear the advisers argue in real time. They show that the president's early instinct was an air strike, that he changed his mind, that his brother and the defense secretary pushed for the blockade, and that Kennedy was more willing to compromise than his public words suggested. They are a reminder that the confident story told afterward is rarely the whole story.

lessons.title: Johnson's Great Society
lessons.mainIdea: Lyndon Johnson used his skill in Congress and a landslide election to pass Medicare, Medicaid, federal school aid and a war on poverty.
reading: Lyndon Johnson took the oath on the plane that carried Kennedy's body home from Dallas. He had spent his life in Congress and knew how to make it move. In 1964 he pushed through the Civil Rights Act that Kennedy had proposed, then won the presidency in November by the largest share of the popular vote in history. He called his program the *Great Society*: a country that would end poverty and racial injustice and give every child a decent education. In 1965 Congress passed more major laws than in any year since the New Deal.

The largest was *Medicare*, health insurance for everyone over sixty-five, paid for through Social Security taxes, along with *Medicaid*, health coverage for the poor paid by the federal and state governments together. Before 1965 about half of older Americans had no health insurance and a serious illness could wipe out a family. The Elementary and Secondary Education Act sent federal money to schools for the first time, targeted at poor districts. Head Start opened preschools for poor children. The Voting Rights Act, which you will study in the next unit, protected the right to vote. New laws opened immigration to Asia, Africa and Latin America for the first time since 1924.

Johnson also declared a *war on poverty*: job training, community action programs run partly by poor people themselves, food stamps and legal aid. The poverty rate fell from about nineteen percent in 1964 to about twelve percent in 1969, and the drop among older Americans was even steeper. Critics on the right argued that the programs were wasteful, that they created dependence and that a booming economy, not government, was lifting people. Critics on the left argued that the war on poverty was never funded seriously and was starved by another war, in Vietnam.

The Great Society also created public television, national endowments for the arts and humanities, the first major laws to clean air and water, and consumer safety rules for cars. Much of it survives; Medicare and Medicaid now cover more than a third of Americans. The argument over it is the same one that began in the 1930s. Illinois today runs Medicaid, spends federal school aid and relies on Head Start, so the debate is not abstract. Every state budget is partly a vote on the Great Society.

lessons.title: The War in Vietnam
lessons.mainIdea: The United States sent more than half a million troops to stop communism in Vietnam, could not win, and lost about fifty-eight thousand lives before leaving.
reading: Vietnam had fought France for independence and won in 1954. The country was then divided, with a Communist government under Ho Chi Minh in the north and an American-backed government in the south. American leaders believed in the *domino theory*: if Vietnam fell to communism, its neighbors would fall one by one. Eisenhower sent aid; Kennedy sent about sixteen thousand military advisers. By 1964 the southern government was losing to Communist guerrillas, the Viet Cong, supplied from the north. In August 1964, after reports of attacks on American ships in the Gulf of Tonkin, Congress gave Johnson broad power to use force. The second attack, it later turned out, probably never happened.

In 1965 Johnson began bombing North Vietnam and sending combat troops. By 1968 there were more than five hundred thousand Americans in Vietnam, most of them drafted, average age nineteen. They fought an enemy that hid among villagers, in tunnels and in jungle, and that could retreat across borders the Americans were not allowed to cross. Success was measured in enemy dead, a number that was often inflated. American bombing dropped more explosives on Vietnam than all sides had used in World War II, and chemicals sprayed to strip the jungle poisoned land and people for decades. Vietnamese deaths, north and south, soldier and civilian, are estimated in the millions.

In January 1968, during the Tet holiday, Communist forces attacked more than a hundred cities across the south at once, even breaching the American embassy in Saigon. Militarily the Tet Offensive failed; the attackers lost tens of thousands. But Americans had been told for years that victory was near, and the pictures on television said otherwise. Support for the war collapsed. In March, Johnson announced he would not run for re-election. That same month, in a village called My Lai, American soldiers murdered hundreds of unarmed civilians, a crime covered up for more than a year.

Richard Nixon, elected in 1968, promised to end the war and instead widened it into Cambodia while slowly withdrawing American troops. In 1971 a leaked secret history, the Pentagon Papers, showed that leaders had doubted the war could be won even as they sent more troops. A peace agreement in January 1973 brought the last American troops home. In April 1975 North Vietnam took Saigon. About fifty-eight thousand Americans had died, their names now carved on a black granite wall in Washington. The war left a deep distrust of government claims that shapes American politics still.

lessons.title: Protest and the Counterculture
lessons.mainIdea: The war and the draft produced the largest antiwar movement in American history and a youth culture that rejected its parents' rules.
reading: Opposition to the war began on college campuses with teach-ins in 1965 and grew with the draft. Young men burned draft cards, fled to Canada or went to prison; the boxer Muhammad Ali refused induction and was stripped of his title. In 1967 about a hundred thousand people marched on the Pentagon. Martin Luther King Jr. came out against the war that year, saying it was draining money from the poor and sending Black men to die for freedoms they did not have at home. By 1969 hundreds of thousands were marching in Washington, and polls showed most Americans thought the war had been a mistake.

The *antiwar movement* argued that the war was unwinnable, that it was killing civilians, and that the government was lying about it. Supporters of the war, still a large group, argued that retreat would abandon an ally and embolden the Soviets and China, and that protesters were undermining soldiers in the field. Families split over dinner tables. Veterans came home to a country that often did not want to hear about what they had seen. In May 1970, after Nixon expanded the war into Cambodia, National Guard troops fired on protesters at Kent State University in Ohio and killed four students. Campuses across the country shut down.

Alongside the protests grew something looser: the *counterculture*. Young people grew their hair, wore what they liked, experimented with drugs, and questioned rules about sex, work and authority. Rock music was its language, from folk singers at protests to the three-day Woodstock festival in 1969. Communes and underground newspapers sprang up. Some of it was serious rethinking of how to live; some of it was fashion. Older Americans, including many who opposed the war, were baffled or angry. Nixon appealed to what he called the silent majority who did not protest and wanted order.

The movements of the era, for civil rights, against the war, for women, for the environment, borrowed from each other and argued with each other. They shared a suspicion of authority that the Pentagon Papers and later Watergate seemed to confirm. Their lasting effects include the end of the draft in 1973, the vote for eighteen-year-olds in 1971, and a permanent change in how Americans dress, talk and question leaders. Their limits are also clear: the war went on for years after most people opposed it, which raises hard questions about how much protest can do.

lessons.title: Chicago, August 1968
lessons.mainIdea: The 1968 Democratic convention in Chicago turned into a televised clash between police and protesters that split the party and helped elect Nixon.
reading: By August 1968 the year had already broken the country's nerve. Martin Luther King Jr. was murdered in Memphis on April 4, and riots burned Chicago's West Side for days; Mayor Richard J. Daley ordered police to shoot to kill arsonists. Robert Kennedy, running for president against the war, was shot dead in Los Angeles in June. Johnson had quit the race. The Democrats came to Chicago's International Amphitheatre to choose between Vice President Hubert Humphrey, who had the delegates and Johnson's war policy, and antiwar senators who had the voters in the primaries.

Thousands of protesters came too, a mix of serious antiwar organizers and theatrical radicals who nominated a pig for president. Daley refused nearly every permit and ringed the hall with barbed wire. He had about twelve thousand police, plus National Guard and Army troops, ready. On the night of Wednesday, August 28, as the convention voted down an antiwar platform, police charged protesters in front of the Conrad Hilton hotel on Michigan Avenue. Television cameras filmed officers clubbing demonstrators, reporters and bystanders. The crowd chanted that the whole world was watching. Inside the hall, a senator from Connecticut denounced Gestapo tactics from the podium while Daley shouted back from the floor.

A government commission studied the week and, in a report written by a Chicago lawyer named Daniel Walker, called what happened a *police riot*: unrestrained violence by police against people who had mostly done nothing to provoke it, while also noting that some protesters had thrown things and taunted officers. Daley's defenders said the police had protected the city from people who came to cause trouble, and polls showed most Americans sided with the police. Eight protest leaders were tried in Chicago on conspiracy charges in a trial that became its own spectacle.

Humphrey was nominated in a hall that smelled of tear gas and lost narrowly in November to Richard Nixon, who promised law and order. Historians see 1968 as the year the New Deal coalition of the 1930s came apart: white working-class voters angry at protesters and riots moved right, while young activists lost faith in the party. Chicago changed its rules afterward, and so did the Democrats, opening the choice of nominees to primary voters. The convention's lessons about protest, policing and cameras are studied every time a city hosts one.
